utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Lazarevic. As you've heard me say to so many people throughout this trial, please bear in mind the solemn declaration to speak the truth continues to apply to your evidence from start to finish. Mr. Bakrac.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, thank you. Good morning, all. Yesterday, I said we would move on to a different topic this morning, but before that, I would like to ask the Trial Chamber, and this is very important for the further presentation of evidence by the Defence of General Lazarevic, the following: We've mentioned that Caragoj Valley once. That's the valley where the Meja action was carried out. And to provide the Chamber with a clearer picture of events, I would like to ask Mr. Lazarevic to explain where this is. We have a map in relief which has no number. It can be marked for identification. And from the Kosovo Atlas, P615, we have a document which we would like to put on the ELMO, by your leave, Your Honours, if I could ask this of General Lazarevic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: There's a map beside the witness. Is that what he is going to refer to?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well if he refers to it, it should be given an in-court number, it wouldn't be marked for identification, so it would become an exhibit in the order.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My mistake, Your Honour. My mistake. I do apologise. I said "marked for identification," but I meant to say "given a number."

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Mr. Lazarevic, General Lazarevic, yesterday we saw a number of exhibits concerning the concentration of KLA terrorists in the Caragoj Valley. Would you be so kind as to show us on this map where the Caragoj Valley is, what large town it's closest to, and where the border with Albania is?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Caragoj Valley, in Serbian it means "Black river," it's a river valley, it's the area between Djakovica and Decani. It belongs to the border belt. It's 10 to 15 kilometers long and 3 to 5 kilometers wide. I will now show where it is [indicates]. Djakovica, Decani [indicates]. This is right behind the border belt. It's actually in the border belt or, rather, in the border area, not the border belt.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Where is the border post there, and what is the terrain like?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: From the Junik Mountains in the direction of the Kosare and Morina border post, there is a very important tactical axes from Albania which was the one most frequently used to infiltrate strong forces for the armed rebellion and later the aggression in the direction of Djakovica, Junik and Decani. From the mountain heights, one can come down and reach the valley in a relatively short period of time.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, General Lazarevic. Could the usher now put this map from the atlas on the ELMO. Perhaps it might be clearer on this map than it is on the relief map.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Indicate what you have just said, and then we will move on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: What is the page number in the Kosovo Atlas, Mr. Bakrac?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 4D471 and 475. It's not clearly visible, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I have this book here that you've put on the screen. Just give me the page number, if you can.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I do apologise. It's 4D471, 475. The map consists of two parts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I take it you don't actually have the book and you can't tell me what page in the book it's in that I can quickly refer to.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: We're finished with that map, anyway, so just leave it on the floor and carry on with the next stage of the exercise.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Mr. Lazarevic, please indicate on the ELMO where the border belt is, where Djakovica is, where the Caragoj Valley is, and where the border posts you mentioned are.

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Indicates]

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Now you're indicating the river valley?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, and the border post to the right is Kosare, and the one to the left is Morina.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Your Honour, could you put the letter "A" above the first arrow and tell us what border post it is?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is Kosare, and the other one is Morina.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, for the purposes of the transcript, the arrow marked "A" leads to the valley through the Kosare border post, and the arrow marked "B" indicates the direction leading to the river valley via the Morina border post. Could this exhibit now be given a number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: First of all, we need to give a number to the large map which was on the board. Can we have that, first of all?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be IC139, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. And then a number for this one --

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It will be IC140.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Before you move on, in an answer, Mr. Lazarevic, at page 2, line 25, for those who are following the transcript, you talked about from the Junik Mountains in the direction of Kosare and the Junik border post, there is a very important tactical," and it's not clear what the next words should be. You were describing a very important tactical something from Albania which was the one most frequently used. Can you clarify what you said there? Were you referring to as a route, an access route, or was it something else?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, in the military sense, it's an area, a valley, within the Junik Mountains, between two border posts, which is suitable for the engagement of military forces, both infantry and armoured and mechanised units, especially those carrying out the attacks. There are no international roads there and no official roads, but I know that right now a motorway is being built between Kosovo and Albania there. But from the military and strategic aspect, it's one of the very important tactical axes along which units, up to two or three brigades, can be engaged for an attack from Albania on the area. And I referred to it as the "Morina tactical axis."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That's clarified it. Thank you. Mr. Bakrac.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Mr. Lazarevic, we'll now move on to another topic. Yesterday, you said that when the forward command post in Djakovica was taken up on the 21st of April, if I'm correct, 1998, until the end of that year, you were constantly at the forward command post in Djakovica. Did you go to Pristina? When and on what occasion, if you did?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Very rarely, only on a few occasions did I leave the forward command post. On orders from the corps commander, I went to the Corps Command to brief him on the situation at the state border, although he often visited the area personally, and to the best of my recollection there was a day in August, I'm not sure exactly when it was, when I went there, and I came back on the same day. In September, I think I stayed away for a day or two because we were preparing plans to defend the state border and an expat report on that topic. I think that in late October, I went there to take over some new officers, and I don't recall going to Pristina on any other occasion.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: When you visited Pristina, as you described, did you attend any other meetings, apart from going to the Corps Command? Did you meet any other people there?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember that with the corps commander and a group of officers and employees of the police and the state security, we went to a civilian building. I'm not sure whether it's the Regional Executive Council, where we exchanged information one evening on the situation in the territory, and several state officials were there, officials of the FRY and of Serbia. I'm not sure who the people from the state security were, what their names were, because I don't know them. At that time, I didn't know the people from the police either, but later on I found out they were assistant Ministers of the Interior, and one of them was General Djordjevic, the other one was Obrad Stefanovic. I don't know whether he's an assistant minister also, but he did have a high-ranking post in the Ministry. I think General Lukic was also there. There may have been some other people as well. And from the state security, I really couldn't tell you their names. And this was more than -- on more than one occasion. I say "several occasions," because in September I stayed there for two or three days. I'm not sure what state officials were there, but in any case, on at least one occasion Mr. Sainovic was there. I saw Andjelkovic, Mr. Andjelkovic. I don't know, as I say, if they were there on both occasions. There was Minic, Matkovic, and, well, that was it.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Mr. Lazarevic, to clarify one point, you say on those two occasions, and then you say once in August and the second time, if I remember well, in September, but you say you stayed there for two or three days. On that second occasion when you visited, did you attend only once or did you go there to that meeting two times in the course of those two or three days?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that in September, while I was there for two or three days, I was with a commander on at least two occasions to see people, to discuss the situation, to exchange information about the situation in Belgrade, in the country, in Kosovo, from the security aspect, from the military aspect, and the police aspect as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: At that meeting, did you speak? And if you did, what did you speak about?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that all the participants were interested in hearing me say firsthand what was happening at the border, and I remember that I did speak, but I really cannot repeat what I said. It was about the situation in the border area, the constant attacks, the extreme threat to the state border. That was the topic I most often spoke about, but I couldn't really paraphrase it right now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: We have to be clear what events we're talking about. You said that on two occasions -- on at least two occasions, you went with the commander to see people to discuss their situation, to exchange information. In that sentence, were you referring to the same group, including police, state security and civil officials, or were you talking about something else?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I was referring to the same group in general, but not the same composition, because I'm not sure that all of those people - I've mentioned some of them by name - were present on both occasions. I was with the corps commander. There may have been someone else from the Corps Command there. This group of people from the Ministry of the Interior, I'm not sure all of them were there at that time. And also I'm not sure whether the state officials were there in full number, whether they were all there in that time. I really couldn't confirm that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Were these meetings each in the same place?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As far as I can remember, yes. It's a room that is similar to this one but perhaps slightly smaller, and I was there on those occasions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... They were in the same place. Now, you've mentioned at least two in September. Were there also similar meetings in August?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I was there only once in August, and then I went back. I didn't spend any time there. So we're talking about one meeting in August, in the same place, dealing with the same issues, with the same groups of people, but I cannot now state whether all the same people were there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now, what about October, when you went to take over some new officers, was there a similar meeting then?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Mr. President, I did not take part. In fact, during the day, I took over the officers, the second lieutenants. I flew to Pristina by helicopter. I took them over and I just dispatched them to their units. I didn't spend any time in Pristina at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Bakrac went on to ask you about what you may have said. Did you speak at only one of these meetings or more than one?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm not sure whether I took the floor on both occasions, but I remember that I did. I remember that I informed those people about the dramatic situation, whether it was in August or in October, but I'm not sure, because the corps commander was there at my side.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Perhaps it's translation, but let's try and not further confuse it. I thought I had got the position clear, but at the moment I'm under the impression there was one meeting in August, at least two meetings in September, and none in October. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, it's a mistake in interpretation. You can listen to the tapes. The whole confusion is caused by the interpretation. August, and two or three occasions in September, when he spent there a couple of days, and then he was in Pristina in October, when he did not attend any meetings but just took over the officers, but the interpretation was that he attended the meetings in August and October. And if you listen to the tapes, you will hear that he said "in September."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That's been clarified, but there's something else you said which caused me some confusion, and that is: "I'm not sure whether I took the floor on both occasions." I thought we had established that there were at least three meetings, and I don't know if that's an interpretation problem or not. Can you remember on how many of these occasions you actually spoke?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, when I say "occasions," I am referring to one occasion in August and another -- or the other in September. But in September, I spent two or three days in Pristina, and in August, I spent only one day -- in August, I attended one meeting. In September, on those two or three days, I attended two meetings. Out of those two meetings, I cannot confirm whether I took the floor every time, but I do remember that I did. Now, whether it was in August or in September, I can't tell you, but I spoke about my firsthand experience from the state border. They wanted to hear what I had to say, because I had come from the border, and this despite the fact that my corps commander was there at my side.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Bakrac.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Mr. Lazarevic, now you've explained everything in quite some detail. What I want to know is: At that meeting, did anyone ever issue any orders to you at those two or three meetings that you spoke about? Did anyone ever issue any orders to you?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: With the Trial Chamber's permission, I have to say the following: It would have been absurd for anyone to issue any orders to me in the presence of the corps commander who was there by my side. So my answer is, no, no one issued any orders to me at that meeting. And now as to --

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: And did anyone issue any orders to the corps commander?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The same answer, nobody was in a position to issue any orders to the corps commander because at that time, as far as I can remember, there were no people present from the Army Command when I was there on those occasions to speak to the corps commander and to issue any tasks to him.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Did the people from the political authorities -- you just explained to us that there were no soldiers there, nobody from the military, but did they issue any orders? You said that there were people from the Ministry of the Interior?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My categorical answer is: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Thank you, General. Now we can move on, unless the Trial Chamber has nothing--

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... the question. I don't know if it's me or others see it the same way. There's a difference between the political authorities in this context and the Ministry of the Interior, is there not?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, it's a misinterpretation. I asked whether anyone from the political structures -- we heard that -- not to the army, gave any orders to the people from the MUP. And I can see now that there's a misinterpretation. I don't know whether we should repeat the answer or whether now everything is clear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I think you should ask -- whatever that question was, you should ask it again, because it's very uncertain at the moment in English.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: General, on the occasions when you attended those exchanges of information and those briefings, did anyone from the political structure present there issue any orders to anyone from the military structure or the structure of the Ministry of the Interior?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I tried to be succinct, but it appears that I failed to explain everything in sufficient detail.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: This question just requires a yes-or-no answer. It's very simple. You'll only confuse the matter further if you try to do more at this stage. If anyone wants more information, they'll ask you. Did anyone from the political structure issue any order to either someone in the Ministry of Interior or someone from the VJ?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let me repeat what I said before. I categorically state no one from the political structures did not issue any orders either to the army or to the police at those meetings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Bakrac.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: General, let's move on. Could we please have Exhibit 3D697 up in e-court. General, in order to wrap this up, we spoke about the actions yesterday and now you spoke about the meetings, do you recognise this document? Could you tell us what is this document that we have in front of us?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I recognise this document because it was used in the trial. This is an analysis of the implementation of the tasks in the Kosovo and Metohija area, which was drafted at the forward command post of the 3rd Army in Pristina on the 2nd of October, 1998, and we have been able to hear who actually drafted it.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Fine, fine, yes, but let us now move to page 2. I would like you to comment briefly on a paragraph in the context of what we've been talking about. So this is the paragraph on page 2, 1.4, "Commanding the Forces." Could you please read it and just comment on it, and tell us whether this is indeed how it was in the field.

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The assessment of the 3rd Army commander regarding the commanding of the forces in this document reads as follows: "For the purpose of commanding the forces of the corps engaged in securing the state border and the border area, the Pristina Corps forward command post was established in Djakovica on the 21st of April, 1998, for the purpose of commanding the entire army in Kosovo and Metohija. The Army forward command post was established in Pristina on the 27th of July, 1998."

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Let us just repeat, this is an analysis dated the 2nd of October, 1998, so that's for the previous period?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: And the actual state of affairs on the ground in Djakovica, did it reflect this analysis or this assessment contained in this analysis?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Thank you, General. Let us just discuss briefly 1998, and then we will move on to 1999. What I want to know is, first of all, how was the Pristina Corps reinforced in 1998, if at all, for the purpose of execution of its tasks?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In 1998, there was a chronic shortage of troops in the Pristina Corps for the execution of the tasks that we were talking about yesterday; securing and defending the state border, securing and defending the facilities and so on. I don't want to enumerate all of them. The 3rd Army Command and the General Staff of the Army of Yugoslavia --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Witness's microphones have been switched off.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's working.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... Sorry about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I was afraid that you switched off my microphone. I expect to do that at a later stage, but now it's a little bit premature, perhaps?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The 3rd Army Command and the General Staff of the Army of Yugoslavia took measures to resolve this issue of the shortage of troops, and I'd say they had a three-pronged approach. They sent new soldiers to the corps to reinforce it. They -- on the orders of the personnel Administration in the General Staff, they sent a certain number of officers down there. They seconded them there. And they also sent some smaller units or elements of units and resubordinated them to the corps for the purpose of the execution of tasks in particular to secure the state border, primarily the border units, the scout units and the military police units.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Could you please tell us, who planned and who approved those reinforcements for the Pristina Corps?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The General Staff of the Army of Yugoslavia made a decision. As far as I can remember, that was as early as in May or in early June that the regular training of soldiers in the corps units should not be carried out, because it was impossible to ensure the security, technical, physical, and organisational aspects. They were to be trained in the training centres outside of Kosovo and Metohija, and after the basic training that was to be completed in the training centres - it lasted for two months and 22 days - they were sent for further training in the corps units. So this was a decision taken by the General Staff. Furthermore, as for the officers, I said a little while ago it was done on the order of the personnel Administration in the General Staff. They were sent there, they were seconded there, for a period between three months and a year. Now, as for the sending of units from the 3rd Army to reinforce the corps, this was done on the orders of the corps commander [as interpreted]. As for the units that were not part of the 3rd Army, they were sent there on the orders of General Perisic, chief of the General Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Since they were sent, we saw how the reinforcement was done, could you please explain to us the system whereby units were resubordinated in the Army of Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it's a complex procedure which is something that is present in all the armies in the world. The Army of Yugoslavia is not an exception. The essence of this process is that a unit is temporarily, for a briefer or longer period of time, leaves its organisational units and becomes part of a new unit. It is resubordinated to that unit, in the sense of the Command, and further -- it's further use for the execution of tasks. It has nothing to do with its original unit, and the original unit has no way of commanding or controlling that unit. Some powers may be retained in personnel, logistics aspects, but as for the use of that unit, any ties between this unit that has been resubordinated and the original unit are severed. And if the Trial Chamber allows me, I will add one more sentence. This process is carried out only in accordance with written orders that regulate this issue in quite some detail; the manner in which the unit is to be resubordinated, the command of that unit, the use of that unit, and everything that has to do with that process. What I mean to say is it cannot be done on an "ad hoc" basis, even when there is a previous plan in place, that there should be resubordination of a unit for a certain task. This is not done automatically before this plan enters into force. Specific orders have to be issued for this resubordination.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: General, you have explained this to us in detail. I'm going to call an exhibit, a document from your brigade that we would like you to comment and show us on this a specific example. Can we have 5D594 brought up in e-court, please. Do you see this document? Can you comment on it for us?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is an order of the Command of the 211th Armoured Brigade, and from what I'm -- the 24th of April, 1999, namely, and it emanated on the basis of my own order dated the 21st of April to the effect that a military territory detachment was from the military district of Pristina was to be resubordinated to that brigade. Upon receipt of my own order, the commander of the brigade issued a precise order to his brigade and to the detachment in question, in terms of how, when, where and in which way it was to be resubordinated and what tasks would be assigned to that military territorial detachment. In item 2, very interestingly the task is described which actually reflects the essence of resubordination. The commander of the military territorial detachment had to report to the commander of the brigade, to his new superior or, rather, to hand over to him a complete report broken down by all combat readiness elements, to familiarise the commander of the brigade with the, shall I say, identity card of the combat readiness of the detachment, not only to report to him orally but also to hand to him over documents about his units, reflecting the combat readiness of his unit. The following bullets -- the following items, define the tasks that is in item 3 and 4, whereas item 5 states that the commander of the Armoured Brigade -- it is to the commander of the Armoured Brigade, that the commander of the detachment shall be responsible thereafter, as of the resubordination date.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: You said "as of that day," General. I wanted to ask you something. The 24th of April, 1999, is the date indicated. Am I right to conclude that military territorial detachments were not all resubordinated in an automatic way, according to a single order, but would be resubordinated to brigade as needed and later during this period; am I right?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You are right. There were detachments until the end of the war that were never resubordinated to brigades but remained subordinated to their basic command, to the command of the military district. This was done successively to correspond to the situation on the ground.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now see another exhibit, please. With this, we wanted to draw a parallel or, rather, to provide an example of resubordination, and now I should like to go back to a document from 1998. This is Exhibit 5D106, and I should like to ask you to comment on items 2 and 5 of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: General, in order to expedite matters, this is an order of the forward command post of the 3rd Army of the 7th of August, 1998. Can you comment on item 2?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As the commander of the army orders that units of the army which are under his command, according to an approved decision, in accordance with the approved decision, may be engaged in support of MUP forces from their deployment areas which are behind the MUP forces formations, through direct action against individual -- namely, selective targets, using armoured/mechanised unit weaponry, artillery or other weapons, but up to a specific calibre. So it is limited to -- the support to MUP forces is limited up to a specific calibre of weaponry.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Can we have page 2 now, and I should like to ask you to comment on item 5.

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The commander of the army, General Samardzic, ordered that in combat operations, combat groups would be directly commanded by brigade commanders or joint task forces, joint tactical units, to which those brigades belong, commanding resubordinated combat groups, namely, those which were assigned from the 3rd Army, outside the corps, or from the entire army, according to the order of the Chief of General Staff, would be regulated by the commander of the Corps by a written order. Resubordination of such combat groups from joint tactical units of the Corps, according to the approval of the army commander, shall be regulated by the corps commander, by written order, meaning that there could be no engagement or resubordination in an automatic fashion, but only in compliance with a strictly-written order.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: General, can there be concerted combat action and coordination with MUP forces without resubordination having been effected at the level of brigade command, and at which level? Your Honours, I heard this and I don't know whether it is in the transcript, but my colleagues are suggesting that you should again explain the "ZTJ" abbreviation. What does this acronym stand for?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: With permission from the Trial Chamber, the "ZTJ" abbreviation means "joint tactical units." Translated to the unit level, this is regiment/brigade-level units. They are joint because they comprise [as interpreted] different arms of the army, different branches [as interpreted].

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: But they are all within the Yugoslav Army?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour. It's page 20, line 10. I believe the witness said: "They are called 'joint' because they compromise different branches of the army," and not "they are called different."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. I think, Mr. Bakrac, your last question at page 20 has not been answered.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honours, I haven't forgotten it. I'm going to go back to it, but we just had an intervention in order to clarify. May we have Exhibit 4D377.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: The question was, while we are waiting for the exhibit to come up, whether there can be coordination action and support for the MUP without previous resubordination.

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In item 2 of the previous document, we saw that the army commander issued an order to the effect that support by the MUP can be carried out only pursuant to a previous order by the commanding officer, because the commander, unless his unit is directly attacked, cannot use the unit without such an order. So the answer to your question is "no," and we have seen the army commander's order to that effect. And if I may, I would also like to say the following: I remember very well an order by the commander of the 3rd Army, General Samardzic, in which he ordered the following: If such an order of his was violated, that he personally should immediately be informed by the brigade commander, passing over the Corps Command, and this was not what was usually done. This is to say that the army could not be used without a previous decision.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: A decision by whom?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: A decision of the corps commander, the army commander, because the army commander retained the exclusive right to provide support by a certain kind of combat technology, so -- so -- this equipment, that is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Bakrac, if we go back to page 21, line 4, "support," should that be "of the MUP" rather than "by the MUP"?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that's right, Your Honour, and my team was about to tell me to intervene. It's "to the MUP," not "by the MUP."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The other question I have is -- again, it may be my misunderstanding of this situation, but so that I'm entirely clear about it, when you talk about resubordination in this context, you're not talking about the MUP being resubordinated; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. We are now showing what is needed for someone to be resubordinated, and then we'll come to 1999 and deal in greater detail with the issue of whether or not there was resubordination. This is now laying the foundation for Your Honours to see what is necessary for resubordination to be carried out.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I answer your question?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Your question has been about resubordination, "Can there be concerted combat action and coordination with MUP forces without resubordination having been effected at the level of brigade command?" And that was in relation to the earlier exhibit. Which units are you talking about being resubordinated?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, my question was the following: "Is there any possibility of carrying out coordinated action and support to the MUP without there being resubordination at any level?"

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The English version of the answer just doesn't answer the question, as far as I can tell. It's one of these questions that probably demands a yes-or-no answer, but instead of that we get several paragraphs, and I'm afraid as it stands at the moment, I do not understand the answer. I don't know about my colleagues, whether they ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: We're not being assisted by this, Mr. Bakrac. We're all, I think, in a state of confusion about resubordination.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: General, please answer this question briefly. Can there be a coordinated action in combat and support to the MUP without any formal resubordination?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, resubordination is a category, a process, whereas coordinated action and support are something else. I said that coordinated action, as Mr. Bakrac said, and support, without going into whether or not there was resubordination, cannot be carried out without a decision of the chief of Staff of the 3rd Army or the corps commander, as can be seen from the document on the screen. It cannot be done, and especially there can be no "ad hoc" resubordination. Someone cannot simply take over a unit of the army or of the police from the brigade commander and resubordinate it for the purposes of a certain task. They cannot do it on their own.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I think I now understand this. What you appear to be saying, and please correct me if my understanding does not appear to be right, what you are saying is that they are two entirely separate processes. And the question that Mr. Bakrac put tends to confuse the two processes. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, you understood this correctly. We were talking about resubordination and touching on these issues, and this will be important later on, when we go on to explain certain things. But I have tried to draw a distinction between support and coordinated action and resubordination, but none of this can be done without numerous written orders.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes. In both cases, specific orders are required, but they are required -- they are orders which have entirely different effects. Have I got that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Absolutely, yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I think I now understand it. Mr. Bakrac, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: I apologise for interfering. Actually, I wish to understand in a simple way what was the de facto position, because a lot of emphasis are being laid on the legal side, on the de jure position, that this cannot be done because until this is done, but we find that there must have been a different de facto position. And you are the best person, sir, to explain to us what really was a reality, and that should not require too much of words or too much of sentences. And I would like to, therefore, beg of you to kindly clarify this position. That would make things more simpler. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the de facto situation in 1998 which I'm referring to was the following: There was coordinated action between the army and the police. There was support provided by -- to the police by the army in combat pursuant to decisions of the Command of the 3rd Army and the General Staff of the Army of Yugoslavia. In 1998, there were no attempts at resubordination, either de jure or de facto.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: I have one further question on this topic before we move on. Can the commander of a unit in the Army of Yugoslavia achieve effective control over a unit which has not been resubordinated to him?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is a legal term, often heard on these premises. From the military point of view, what I'm trying to say is the following: The process of command and the system of command has its process functions, one of which is control. If the first functions are missing of organising, planning, commanding, or as the NATO standards say, power over a unit or authority over a unit, then there can be no control and no effective control. It's absolutely impossible, therefore, to achieve effective control over someone unless you have the right to command that structure or to have authority or power, as the NATO standards say, over that structure.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: General, let's move on now to a new topic, which we'll deal with very briefly. In your experience as chief of Staff in 1998, what was the cooperation like between the OSCE and the Pristina Corps?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If we are referring only to 1998, the OSCE mission was completed or brought up to full numbers only at the end of the year, but there was another mission there, the Kosovo diplomatic mission, KDOM. And from my point of view and from what I know, and from my activities in 1998, my assessment of that cooperation is that it was in compliance with the agreement between our country and the OSCE and KDOM. If I have to put it in a nutshell: In my personal experience, only on two occasions in 1998 did I have personal contacts with the OSCE mission. That was in December, when I attended a meeting attended by Mr. Dirankevic [phoen] and his team. I was present at the meeting, but I didn't take the floor. A team from the Army Command was there. And on the 13th of November, I remember well, when there had been a terrorist attack on an army column in the Dulja area, I personally asked that the British military attache arrive, Colonel Crosland, to verify the murder of a soldier and the serious act of terrorism. I hope Your Honours will not hold it against me if I say that, in a way, I was pleasantly surprised when, after this massacre which took place, Crosland and I signed a joint record establishing that this had been a serious terrorist attack on an army unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: And was that army unit in a location that had been provided for in the agreement?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Oh, no, that was a convoy. It was a bus full of soldiers on their way from Nis to the Djakovica garrison. The soldiers had been on leave. In front of that bus, there was a transport vehicle in which there were soldiers who were providing security, and hand-held rocket-launchers were loosed at close proximity to open fire on that column and kill those people.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: General, were there any weapons inspections at the Pristina Corps in accordance with the agreement between NATO and the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember quite clearly all those inspections, and I took part in the drafting of the report and in preparing the units in Metohija for this very important inspection. My personal knowledge is that there were some 30 such inspections and that on no occasion were there any objections on the part of the NATO mission verifiers. These were primarily verifications or inspections of the anti-aircraft rocket weapons that had been immobilised. They were sealed, there were numbers affixed, and the verifiers controlled all that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: General, could you please look at 5D72. It's an exhibit. It appears to be a document that you drafted. Is this a document that deals with precisely this issue that you were talking about?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this is the telegram that I sent from the forward command post in late October to the 3rd Army Command. I was authorised to do so by the corps commander. In it, I report to the 3rd Army Command that all the units of the Pristina Corps -- that the rocket units, as indicated here, Strela 1M and Strela 2M, had been disengaged, and prepared for the inspection to be carried out by the mission, and that special documents had been put together that will be placed at their disposal for their perusal.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: General, let us move on now. Was the cooperation between the Pristina Corps and the OSCE mission verified in any way by the General Staff of the Army of Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember that in late 1998, a large team came, and they controlled a large number of teams that were tasked to cooperate with the OSCE mission within the Corps, but there were also some individual controls carried out by smaller teams. But I remember this control quite vividly, because some aspects of the agreement had been clarified. So there were such controls from the army level and from the General Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: And what was their assessment of the cooperation on the part of the Pristina Corps?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In 1998 and in 1999, I never heard of any objections to any units in the Corps, in the sense that they were failing to comply with the instructions that were drafted at the level of each brigade, how they should treat the mission, or with the provisions of the protocol. I don't know of any major objections. There were, of course, some minor defects, deficiencies, but nothing major, or at least I don't know about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, in order to move forward more quickly, I would just like to point the Trial Chamber's attention to documents that have already been admitted into evidence, 3D787 and 408. They deal with those controls.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: General, sir, just one more question. I would like us to comment on something that is already in 3D407. Was a joint team of the Pristina Corps and the 3rd Army set up for the cooperation with the OSCE mission? I'm asking you this because a Prosecution witness, Witness Ciaglinski, told us something about the replacement of Colonel Kotur, that he was removed from that position, so now perhaps you could explain to us whether any such joint team had been set up and whether Colonel Kotur had been replaced.

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is true that a single team was set up, the team of the 3rd Army and the Pristina Corps, in early March on the orders of the chief of the General Staff of the Army of Yugoslavia, but it is not true -- it is definitely not true that anyone removed Colonel Kotur from that team.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Thank you, General. What relationship did the Pristina Corps have with the International Community representatives, if there were any such contacts?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, there were -- there was plenty of contacts in the 150 days of the mission, approximately 150 days that the mission was in existence. I have this information in my head. It may not be completely accurate, but I hope that the Trial Chamber will not hold it against me. There were over 180 meetings of the liaison teams from the Corps with the representatives of the OSCE mission and KDOM, 180 meetings where a number of issues from the agreement were discussed. Furthermore, there were dozens of inspections of the corps units by the verifiers. I told you already about the number of weapons inspections carried out by the KDOM mission. There were dozens, more than 30 or 40, occasions where terrorist attacks against the army were verified to have occurred. The verifiers came, they verified those attacks. They were present during the drills, the target practise. They were even present at various feasts when new soldiers were brought in or soldiers were -- farewell parties for soldiers, but I don't want to go into that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Yes. Perhaps we are now going into too much detail.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Lazarevic, did Colonel Kotur have command responsibilities within the 3rd Army or was he exclusively tasked with being a liaison with the KVM?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, Colonel Kotur is the chief of the infantry organ in the Pristina Corps. He is not a member of the 3rd Army Command. And in addition to this function -- this is not a command function within the Corps Command. It is a planning function. He focused his activities on the liaison between the Pristina Corps and the OSCE mission, and within that liaison organ he had two other officers that carried out day-to-day duties of the infantry organ within the Pristina Corps Command.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Bakrac.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: General, did it ever happen that the KLA members would exploit the presence of the foreign diplomats, foreign representatives, or journalists to attack the Army of Yugoslavia units?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'd say unfortunately, yes. Unfortunately, because there were such occasions, and I remember that in February, in the vicinity of Mitrovica, a foreign reporter was at risk because he was with the terrorists and they carried out this exercise, this simulated attack, and his life was in risk. So there were such cases.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It appears to me that the transcript may lead one to an erroneous conclusion that the attacks were launched by the reporters or the international representatives, but in fact it was -- they were carried out by the terrorists in the presence of those foreign reporters and representatives.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I see what the transcript says, Mr. Bakrac. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: General, now I want -- we saw an exhibit here, and it was analysed. Could we please put P969 up on the screen. Could you comment on it? It appears to be an order issued by you in 1998. Could you please look at it closely and comment on it? Tell us what it is and what the purpose was behind the drafting of such an order.

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Have you read it?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I've seen it. I know what this is all about. This is an order issued at the forward command post in mid-July 1998, where I warn the units that a large number of diplomats and international representatives will be present throughout Kosovo and that the terrorist forces will exploit their presence and will try to cause incidents, to attack the army units in order to provoke the units, the corps units, into responding, and threatening the lives of the international representatives. I ordered that before there was any response to such attacks, that there should be additional reconnaissance of the area from which the attack had come, and if the presence of any international representatives is established in the vicinity of the terrorist forces, that there should be no response to those attacks in order to save their lives and to avoid any consequences that might endanger the lives of those international representatives. I mean to say that we sincerely cared for the security of the international representatives, even when our personal safety was at stake. This is the essence of this order. I'd say this is a warning of a sort as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Were there any similar orders issued by the corps commander regarding --

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreters note, could the speakers please not overlap.

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We repeatedly issued such orders. I remember that there were several such orders. This order was drafted within the Corps chain of command, and quite naturally the corps commander personally issued orders of this nature, and so did the subordinate units on the basis of those orders.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Also in order to prevent any danger to the civilian population and international observers?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Here we're talking about the observer missions, but there are many such orders that pertain to the civilian population.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Could you please read a part of this for us, Mr. Lazarevic. Immediately before the word "Order 1 and 2", there is a sentence which includes a reference to Siptar terrorists. Could you read that sentence, please? Read it out loud.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] "In order to prevent any uncontrolled and unnecessary fire from being opened on the part of the corps units against the Siptar terrorists, I hereby order: Order:"

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And could you now read number 2, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] "If the situation demands that fire must be returned to protect the lives of the members of the Corps, take measures to open fire from the same kind of weapons in order to avoid returning infantry fire with tank cannon fire and so on."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: What's the purpose of that last reference, because in its context it suggests that if the KVM were not present, then it would be okay to respond to infantry fire with tank cannon?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] With all due respect, Your Honour, on the basis of this document and what I wanted to say, because I drafted this order, the essence is in the first item here: Fire should not be opened at all if the presence of international representatives is observed. And in item 2, it is indicated that if it cannot be avoided, fire should be opened selectively and in a reduced -- at reduced level. In answer to your question, whether fire would be opened from tanks to respond to infantry fire in any other case, I have to tell you that it is not economic, in military terms. It is financially not expedient at all to respond with tank fire to infantry fire.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Well, it's now an appropriate place, I hope, to interrupt, Mr. Bakrac. It's certainly a suitable time.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: We'll adjourn for 30 minute 20 minutes until 10 minutes to 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Bakrac.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. Prior to proceeding, I should like to ask for a correction to be entered in the transcript. That is page 16, lines 5 and 6. The transcript says that as regards reinforcements from the 3rd Army, that is ordered by the corps commander, and I believe what it should read: "It is ordered by the commander of the 3rd Army."

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm going to say something, Your Honours, which is not out of courtesy for the interpreters, whose job is extremely difficult, and they also have to cope with the overlapping of answers and questions and handle various military terminology. I fully appreciate that, but I do request the Trial Chamber, given the importance of this testimony for us, for special attention to be paid to the re-listening of these tapes when that is being done. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Bakrac, I'm sure that the same attention is given to the tapes of all witnesses. That's a vital aspect of the work of the Tribunal. I understand your concern, but I have every confidence that the tapes will be carefully reviewed, as they are on all occasions. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. Mr. Lazarevic had responded that there will be a number of orders similar to this one, P169. I should like to refer the Court to the Exhibit 5D1172, which is a similar order of the corps commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: General, did the Command of the Pristina Corps, as far back as in -- as late April 1998, issue an order on the application of the Geneva Conventions regulations and the provisions of the International Law of War, and was the concept of civilian population interpreted in that context?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember this one special order. I would stress "special" because it dealt with the application of the International Law of War and the Geneva Conventions in peacetime during conflicts with terrorist forces. Let me not go into legal categories, because these forces do not fall within the categories dealt with in these conventions. But, nevertheless, the Command of the Corps felt that it was necessary to issue a specific order to its units to the effect that they should comply with all those conventions and the provisions of International Humanitarian Law.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Will counsel please not overlap with the answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Bakrac, let's deal with the intervention of the interpreter just now. There was no allowance made there for the completion of the interpretation before you proceeded with the next question, and you really must do that. In view of what you said earlier, it's incumbent on you to assist the interpreters as far as possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I fully agree, and I said a while ago that I appreciate the difficulties that I'm causing the interpreters. But you must understand that I am between hammer and anvil. I am always fearing that you might reproach me for wasting time, not proceeding fast enough, but I will certainly seek to wait for the end of the interpretation, whilst, on the other hand, seeking to expedite matters and economize in this case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It's very important, Mr. Bakrac, that you ensure that Mr. Lazarevic's case is fully presented to the Court, and a particularly important aspect of that is his own evidence. So we all have a responsibility here to ensure that he has adequate opportunity to do so, and he will be given adequate opportunity.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: General, please look now at Prosecution Exhibit 51535. Your Honours, the transcript does not contain the answer because of the difficulties of the interpreter, so I'm going to open this document. And I am going to ask you again, and we are going to overcome that, thereby, and proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is Prosecution Exhibit P1535.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Do you see this exhibit which is before you on the screen? Would you be so kind as to tell us what kind of a document this is?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is an order of the Pristina Corps Command, dated the 29th of April, 1998, and it refers to regulating the question of the application of the regulations of the International Law of War, the Geneva Conventions and other regulations in the actions of members of the Corps in executing their peacetime tasks. Unfortunately, it was peace, but practically it was war because we had terrorism active in Kosovo and Metohija, and that is why this order was issued. When I say "war," I don't mean it in the literal sense of the war, because the terrorist side was not a participant in the conflict according to international conventions. That is why, in my introductory part, I said this was a very important order of the Corps Command. If you would like me to comment on the individual items, I can do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Please look at page 2, item 3, to see whether it envisages the treatment of the civilian population and procedures in connection with monuments of culture and similar.

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This order also invokes regulations on the application of the Rules of International Law of War in the Yugoslav Army, and it is an official document in the Yugoslav Army and, as such, regulates primarily relations of the army members towards the civilian population, towards captured enemies, towards property, in terms of forbidding entry into inhabited places. And very importantly in item 3, there is an explanation of what is meant under the concept of "civilian population." With permission from the Trial Chamber, I could comment on some of these elements. Shall I continue?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: I believe that no comment is required, because the document is self-explanatory. We can read it all, in it, unless there's something specific that you would like to add?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: With permission from the Trial Chamber, I would like to say something, because this involves international standards and norms, these are copied international standards. A civilian person is not a civilian person, according to international standards of the Geneva Convention, if such a person should find him or herself with a military formation or unit or beside a military unit, or if it is found in or by a military facility. I should like to say that over and -- we acted over and above this standard, which is evident from the previous orders; namely, we practically did not abide by these international standards in that sense. We never opened fire at civilians and at terrorists. In fact, when civilians were with them and in such a situation, a civilian is actually deprived of his status of civilian, loses his state of civilian, if he is in the company of terrorist forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Thank you, General. I have another question in this connection, and then we will move on to 1999. What was the attitude or, rather, the assessment of the General Staff of the Yugoslav Army and the further state organ in respect of the method, the way in which the Yugoslav Army was engaged in Kosovo and Metohija, specifically in terms of compliance with International Humanitarian Law in 1998?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Here we have two questions. What was the attitude of the General Staff and that of the state organs? In my personal experience, in all my inspection tours of units in Metohija, and in particular of the Djakovica region, where I was, there were over 20 of such tours, and there were also five tours by the chief of the General Staff. I never heard from any of the team members of the General Staff or the chief of the General Staff himself, General Perisic, that they had any objections in respect of the conduct of the Corps members, and I did have occasion, in the previous period, to see in the documents that he assessed that the Corps units in Kosovo and Metohija, in 1998, behaved or comported themselves in a professional manner. As regards your second question, I know from the media, the written media and electronic media, that in September or October, as far as I can remember, both assemblies, the Assembly of Serbia and the Assembly of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, issued special communiques in which they expressed gratitude and honoured the army and the police for having professionally discharged -- for professionally discharging their tasks in Kosovo and Metohija in defending the integrity of the country in Kosovo and Metohija in 1998.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. In order to save time, I am going to refer to you some exhibits, that is, 1D202, 2D67 and 3D757.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: General, we are now going to move on. At a certain point yesterday, we referred to the KLA's preparations for what is known as the "spring offensive." According to your information, what was the KLA's strategy in early 1999?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Regrettably, in the presence of the international mission at Kosovo and Metohija, already at the beginning of 1999, the armed rebellion was gaining momentum and was escalating on the basis of the strategy -- of their strategy, the strategy being to actually speed up the escalation of terrorism and the armed rebellion throughout Kosovo and Metohija in order to convince, persuade and compel, force, the Albanian population by the KLA for a repeated -- a renewed armed conflict with their own state, and to, by widespread violence throughout Kosovo and Metohija, impress it upon different international factors that it was necessary for this internal conflict to assume, as soon as possible, the proportions -- the characteristics of an international one, and the ultimate objective of that strategy was to achieve the long-ago-proclaimed objective of a succession of a part of Serbia, that is to say Kosovo and Metohija, from its parent country of Serbia, with the aid of international factors. So this strategy was a further expansion of terrorism, escalation of it, employing all these methods, targeting the security forces, but in particular also the civilian population.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Did you have any information that the KLA was mobilising able-bodied young men?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As early as the beginning of February, 1999, there was a public proclamation going around, and I asked that this not be held against me, when I say "so-called," by the so-called General Staff, because they declared themselves to be the General Staff of the KLA, calling for a general mobilisation of Albanians in Kosovo and Metohija and in the diaspora. A large number of verified facts were received by the Command of the Corps and the Command of the 3rd Army about forced mobilisation, especially in rural areas in Kosovo and Metohija.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we have on e-court 3D1052.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: General, this is a report by the 3rd Army Command, the Security Section, of the 13th of March, sent urgently to the Security Administration of the General Staff of the Yugoslav Army. Can you comment on item 2.2? Does this refer to what you just said, that in early February there was already a proclamation going around?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, item 2.2 contains information about the forced mobilisation of the Albanian population in the areas of Prizren, the villages around Prizren, by the KLA, and the moving out -- the migration of the Albanian population in order to avoid forced mobilisation. I'm drawing attention to the fact that there is specific mention of the villages of Korisa and Kabas overlooking the barracks in Prizren, where there was a danger that the barracks of the 549th Motorised Brigade might be attacked. They forcibly mobilised the population, and whenever they could, they fled, as this information shows.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: General, were there attempts to place explosives in order to create insecurity among the population, and were other similar methods used? Did you have information about this, and how did you receive such information?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the Corps Command and in the 3rd Army Command, we had, as we say, operative information, our own information about the preparation of armed rebellion forces for terrorism, and in February and especially March, unfortunately this came about. We also received official -- when I say "official information," I mean it came from the OSCE. It was specific information from the OSCE in early March, saying that the terrorists were preparing six large actions, using large explosive devices in urban areas, and there was mention of Pristina, the markets in Pristina, and the terrorists told the verifiers that they would do something big, something like Racak and Markale. I'm trying to paraphrase what the OSCE members told our liaison teams.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: General, we'll come back to this document and to page 2 of this document to see what actually happened, but now could we have on e-court Exhibit 5D636. This -- well, I'm just waiting for the English translation to come up. This is a document from the 3rd Army Command, from the liaison team. The date is the 5th of March. Could you please take a look at page 2, item 3. Is this the information you were referring to that was received from the OSCE?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: If I may, I know Mr. Bakrac has mentioned the English translation, but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: We understand that, Mr. Hannis. There's no English translation of this, Mr. Bakrac.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, forgive me, it's my mistake. I thought the translation had come up on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Could you please read item 3 on page 2, just read the sentence up to the end of the paragraph?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I'm sorry. If I may, Your Honour, when I checked on e-court for this document, it seemed to indicate there was an English translation, however I got the message "Denied," which I understand is what happens when it hasn't been released by the Defence. So if there is an English translation, I would ask that it be released so we can look at it now.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, my team members are now telling me that there is a translation. It's been linked, it's been disclosed in e-court. It may be a technical problem in opening it. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis tells us that it's not been released and that it's you who have control over its release.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: My case manager tells me that now we have it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It's magic. Let's continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, now we can see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Could you please read item 3 on page 2, up to the end.

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "'KLA threats'," in quotation marks, "that they will carry out large-scale actions, something large-scale, "(large-scale massive operations)," in brackets, "in Racak and Markale, several sources have put out information that the terrorists have six huge explosive devices that they intend to use in an urban area, possibly in Pristina." Two markets are being mentioned. "The OSCE mission representative said that everything would be done to prevent this."

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Thank you, General. Let's now go back to Exhibit 3D1052, page 2. As we've already seen page 2, I wish to remind everyone that this is a report by the 3rd Army Command, the Security Department, sent urgently to the Security Administration of the Main Staff of the Army of Yugoslavia, dated the 13th of March, 1999. Could you please read item 2.7, item 2.8, and the first two paragraphs?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Excuse me, 2.7 or 2.8?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: First 2.7 and then 2.8.

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "At around 14.20 hours on 13 March 1999, an unidentified explosive device exploded at the Kosovska Mitrovica marketplace, killing two individuals and wounding 34 others, some seriously, others slightly, including two Serbs who were slightly wounded." Item 2.8: "At 13.05 hours on the 13th of March, 1999, in the neighbourhood of Njegeseva Street near the Podujevo police station, an explosive device with great destructive power exploded, wounding six people." And then it says: "At 13.20 hours on the 13th of March, 1999, an explosive device exploded in the JNA Street, killing three people and wounding nine, some seriously, others slightly. Among the wounded was a Serb, who sustained slight injuries."

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: General, were such situations and such escalation of terrorism widespread, were they widespread occurrence, because here we've mentioned Kosovska Mitrovica, Podujevo?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: By Their Honours leave, I wish to say that the OSCE mission had good intentions when, at a meeting with our team, they tried to say that they would prevent such crimes. However, about ten days later, on a single day, the 13th of March, in two towns on three locations, about 40 civilians were either killed or wounded. So my answer is affirmative. There were such attacks and crimes a little before that in Orahovac, in the center of town, then in Pristina and throughout Kosovo and Metohija, focusing on urban areas. And as I have already said, we were informed by the verifiers that the terrorists would transfer their activities to urban areas, as they told them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Lazarevic, can you explain to me why it is in these reports that if there is a Serb involved as a victim, that that is specifically noted?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, all I can say at this point in time is what my opinion is, because I'm not the author of this document. But one can see from this that the intention of the perpetrators was against civilians. In Podujevo at that time, Your Honour, there were barely a hundred Serbs. Only one was left, and that one became a casualty. I can't really say, with precision, what the author of this document meant.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: General, perhaps the author wanted to say that among the victims, there were also Serbs, in order to avoid implications --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Don't answer that question. That's the most blatant of leading questions in an area that we were trying to explore to actually see if it might produce assistance for us, because what really matters here is -- well, I suspect one of the things that matters here is who's actually being targeted, and you've often made the point for the Defence that the KLA targeted Albanians, but it doesn't seem to be the explanation for the reference to the Serb who gets the cut finger when two other people are killed and many others are seriously injured. It's a not uncommon feature the world over for the press to be concerned about their own population. There's a well-known story in Scotland of the sinking of the Titanic, and the headline in the newspaper was: "Man feared lost overboard in Atlantic," and we all know subsequently of the numbers who died. Now, that's understandable in the context of national reporting, but one of the points that is often made in this case is that we are all the population of Serbia. But here we have reports distinguishing Serbs who are slightly wounded, and I wondered why that happened. But there doesn't seem to be a clear explanation at the moment, so please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: General, tell me, did you have any information about the -- well, first of all, did NATO bring some forces to Macedonia in 1999, and if it did, how do you know this?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, if they had brought some forces, that would not have been a problem, but they brought elite combat forces from several member states of the NATO alliance as early as February to Macedonia in an area close to the border with the FRY, towards the territory of Kosovo and Metohija, and they had a mission. Very soon, that mission was changed and transformed into an open threat to the security of the FRY. So to answer your last sub-question, we had intelligence from the General Staff and from the 3rd Army and from our border units, and we also had operative information from the organs and services whose task it is to obtain such information. We knew the number of tanks and we knew where these forces were deployed.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, lest we should now open a document that contains several pages, let me just give you a reference. That's 5D105. That's for your reference, Your Honours. This is a document from the Security Administration of the General Staff about the situation in the region, the forecasts of the developments, and their influence on the combat readiness of the Army of Yugoslavia in 1999.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: General, let us deal with this issue quickly. You started telling us about the figures, so what was the strength of this force and what kind of equipment did they have?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
