utterances.text: The forces deployed in Macedonia were part of a larger contingent, so let me first answer regarding the strength of the ground forces in Macedonia. That was over 12.000, 12.500 troops, 350 tanks and personnel carriers, over 130 artillery pieces. They also had helicopters. But that was just the ground forces. A part of the overall mission included over -- the deployment of over 40 warships. Several hundred cruise missiles were also assigned for this mission, so let me not go into that. Over 400 warplanes in terms of the Air Force. So this was all one mission.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The English translation refers to something called the 300 -- maybe a part of it is off the screen. Just give me a second. No, the position is clear, in fact. Thank you. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: General, before these forces were deployed in Macedonia on the same axis, the Djeneral Jankovic-Kacanik axis, had there been any infiltrations of terrorist groups; do you know about that?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would like to say, first of all, that NATO forces had already been deployed in Kosovo or, rather, in Macedonia, when the attacks by strong terrorist forces from Macedonia escalated along this axis, Djeneral Jankovic-Kacanik and the Globocica-Kacanik crossing. That was in late February and early March.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: General, since we have heard evidence from a protected witness in this case, and we also heard evidence from other witnesses, I would like you to comment. Let us open Exhibit 3D1048, and could you please comment on paragraph 1, the situation at the border.

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this a report from the security department in the 3rd Army sent to the security administration and the General Staff of the Army of Yugoslavia on the 2nd of March, 1999. In paragraph 1, the description is given of an event of an incident on the previous day. It was an incursion of a strong terrorist force numbering 200 terrorists, the subsequent conflict with our border control organs in the depth of the security belt, and the killing of an officer from the 72nd Special Brigade, because an element from that brigade had been engaged to secure the state border. That was Mirjacic. He was a staff sergeant.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You Honour, Witness K-73 testified about this incident, for your reference.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Would you be so kind as to look at paragraph 2.1 and 2.2 and to comment on those two paragraphs.

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Certainly. At that time, there was a large concentration of terrorist forces who had come from other flashpoints, primarily from Malisevo and Jezerska Mountain to the Kacanik area, and the villages in the border belt and the border area, the villages that are mentioned in the crime base, in the indictment, were effectively turned into terrorist strongholds, and soon the civilian population would be expelled from those villages and forced to go to Macedonia. This we will see from documents that we will follow. Paragraph 2.2 indicates that at that time period in early March, but that also was the case in late February, in the center of the town of Urosevac, which is on this axis, Macedonia-Kacanik-Urosevac-Jezerska Mountain, that there were village watches, village guards, the security, that the KLA was arming people in the town. And in our assessment, a corridor was being set up from the Macedonian border, and the operational and strategic objective, as far as we were concerned, was quite clear. That was in order to be able to bring in the multinational forces from Macedonia into this area using this axis.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: In paragraph 2.5, this report states that there is knowledge of the location where the KLA members are, Retimlje, Orahovac, where their headquarters is located. Is this intelligence correct?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This key corridor, this key axis leading from Macedonia, where there was this large NATO force, leads from Kacanik to Urosevac to Jezerska Mountains, to Orahovac, and then on to Drenica. In early March, the terrorist activities and the activities of the armed rebels escalated already, and these were facts that had been established.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Lazarevic, is there any actual tangible evidence of NATO support or assistance to any of these rebel groups?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, we at the Corps Command, and I hope that we will be able to see evidence here in court, really had at our disposal information about the direct collusion between the multinational forces that were part of the NATO force in Macedonia with the armed rebels. This took shape of instructions -- I don't want to use the word "order," I'm saying "instructions," what areas to take, but unfortunately some members of the OSCE mission formed a third point in this triangle. So we did have the information.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I was thinking more of the example of which we have heard some evidence, that weapons of Chinese manufacture, which could have made their way through Albania, may have been found at certain locations where there was terrorist activity. Now, is there any evidence of that kind that might -- or anything similar that might suggest direct involvement of NATO in this idea here that there should be a corridor created through which the land forces would occupy Kosovo, or are you simply relying on intelligence about what they might have had in mind?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, we did have, I'd say, highly-reliable operational intelligence from sources in Macedonia about the activities of NATO along this axis, but during the war we arrested or captured, in fact, because it was in wartime, in an area close to the Macedonian border, two terrorists who had been in direct communication with NATO forces, providing them with the axes they could use to infiltrate their forces. In addition to Chinese weapons, the KLA had very modern NATO-standard anti-armour weapons. They had long-range sniper rifles, grenade launchers and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: General, let us wrap up as far as this document is concerned. Could we please look at paragraph 2.6, and if we could hear your comments on it?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Paragraph 2.6 deals with something that we've already discussed, the tactics, two villages that was employed by the terrorists, where the terrorists expelled the villagers from the village of Pirane, turning it into a terrorist stronghold in late February. This village is at the Prizren-Djakovica main road. This road goes on to Orahovac. And I know that for a fact they launched attacks on anyone or anything that moved along that road. And by your leave, Your Honours, just one more sentence. During the war, both I and the army commander passed by that village, and we were under crossfire from the terrorists. They opened fire at us from that village.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: General, before the war started in 1999, did you have an assessment as to the strength of the KLA immediately on the eve of the aggression and the level of their organisation?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Before the aggression against our country started and before the armed rebellion in Kosovo and Metohija escalated fully, we had quite specific information both as to the strength and as to the concentration of the armed rebel forces. The strength ranged, as it did in mid-1998, between 20.000 and 25.000, and the operation -- that was the operational component, and the flashpoints were the same as in 1998, Lab, Drenica, Malisevo, Djakovica, Kacanik, Jezerska Mountains, the whole of Metohija, in fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please have Exhibit 5D1335 in e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: And perhaps you might comment, in this context, what that document is all about. Could we just zoom in a little bit, and perhaps zoom out a little bit so that we can see what's here on the left-hand side. That's fine. General, could you please tell us, what is this that we see in front of us on the screen?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a map with an overview which was made at the Corps Command. It was used during the war. The left-hand side, the table, was actually done after the end of the war, after the military pulled out of Kosovo and Metohija, and this is information obtained from KFOR. We compared our information that we had during the war, and we realised that the two sets of figures tallied to a great extent. KFOR produced their own map, and their information indicates that the KLA had more brigades and more people than we assessed.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: So this is an overview of the deployment?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Operative zones and brigades of the Siptar forces -- Siptar terrorist forces in Kosovo and Metohija until the end of the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: General -- Your Honours, it is -- what is missing in the transcript is "from the 23rd of March until the end of the war." General, did the OSCE, and if it did, how did it assess the situation, because we can see that their representatives were in Kosovo and Metohija until the 20th of March?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In early March, especially after the attacks mounted in urban milieus with explosive devices, the OSCE expressed concern for the general security situation in Kosovo and Metohija, and I do feel that this was a genuine concern for the overall situation, that of the OSCE, that is, because they also conveyed this information to our teams and discussed ways to prevent a wholesale escalation of the conflict. So they did have such information, and it is my personal assessment, pursuant to the reports submitted to me by the liaison team, that they were concerned for the overall situation, security situation in Kosovo, on account of the escalating terrorism in Kosovo and Metohija.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Was it their assessment that ceasefire violations by the KLA and their attacks could jeopardise the peace processes that were being conducted in early 1999?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have information that they communicated their assessments to our teams. They demanded and occasionally kindly requested, despite the extreme restraint of the army, but they actually did ask the army to find the strength to refrain and to prevent the violence from spiraling further.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, in order for us not to look into each of these documents individually, I will refer you to the Prosecution exhibits, which are Prosecution Exhibit P638, P649 and P680. These are OSCE reports which show that this was the kind of information that obtained.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: While at the subject of the OSCE mission, which we shall shortly wrap up and move on, to your engagement, the engagement of the Corps and concrete orders, will you please just comment on this: There was -- there were different comments, General Maisonneuve, inter alia, and this concerns document P772 [as interpreted], and this is a map of the deployment of combat groups in the area, which -- in association with the deployment agreement. The number is 2772. That should be rectified in the transcript, P2772. And MM-9, that is a map of the Yugoslav Army units. Your Honours, perhaps it would be better if we put this map on the ELMO, because we will expedite matters in that way. And if the usher would be so kind as to place this on the ELMO, I think that would be the more expedient way to proceed. Colleague Hannis is familiar with this map. It is MM-9 in Exhibit P2772, and I hope that he has no objection to us proceeding in this way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Is P2772 the statement of Maisonneuve?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honours, and it is with a statement attached to MM-9 and it is actually page 85 in e-court. Colleague Petkovic has just helped me identify the right page in e-court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can it be rotated, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: General, could we have your comment on this sketch or map which represents -- which should represent the VJ -- the Yugoslav Army out of barracks?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The chief of the Regional Centre of the OSCE Mission number 5 for Prizren, General Maisonneuve, showed this map with his statement where it represents, in 14 locations, the deployment of the individual units of the Yugoslav Army in the area of Kosovo and Metohija. I do not know what period this refers to, but I presume that it concerns the period prior to the aggression, January, February, and including March. I have the following explanation, and I have to follow a certain order in this. On the bottom side or, as we say, on the southern side and the western side, or southwest side, are shown the locations of units which all are in the depth security belt of the state border. I should like to underline that Maisonneuve showed the city of Djakovica with two lines above the rectangle, which means that this is a unit of battalion rank, whereas this is a barracks, and it is not only out of barracks, going --

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Mr. Lazarevic, I -- I'm sorry to interrupt you. It is hard for the interpreters to follow. Please slow down a bit.

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All right. Junik-Decani, in the sector of Junik there was a combat group for the depth security of the state border -- in-depth security, which Ciaglinski himself toured in January and that he confirmed here during his testimony. The next rectangle is Volujak. That is the disposition or the deployment of a combat group, a mixed company, 145 men strong, according to the agreement. Then northward, there is Lapusnik and Komorane, the two rectangles which are at the location of just one unit from the 15th Armoured Brigade, which was composed of two elements of disperse, and that was also in compliance with the agreement.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Sorry, when you say "was comprised of two components," can you explain?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can explain. One of the elements of this company was on the right-hand side of the road, in the region of the farm, and the second element was on the left-hand side of the road, in the area which was a forested -- a woody area. That is, under the agreement, one and the same unit which was regularly inspected by the KVM mission verifiers. On the extreme north, it is written "Bajgora." That is a facility of significance for the defence of the country, as it is referred to in the document. That is a stationary communications node or a communications centre which is a military facility where a platoon is securing the facility after the incident with a kidnapping of eight soldiers or -- in the beginning of January 1999. And then we have Vucitrn. In Vucitrn, I suppose this does not refer to the Vucitrn barracks but to the exercise ground where, for some 10 or 15 days, exercises were being carried out, and these exercises were regularly monitored and seen by the mission -- OSCE mission from Djakovica. Then we have Podujevo eastward, and that is the company which was part of the Batlava Airport, where there were regular exercises, and this unit was toured by Mr. Drewienkiewicz, himself, repeatedly. And then further on eastward we have Stimlje, but I should also like to draw your attention to Dulja down south. Maisonneuve showed two circles and two rectangles for one and the same location, because that is one combat group, according to the agreement. One part was at the entrance to the Crnojevska Gorge and the other was at the Dulja Pass. They were securing the Crna Klisura, the "black gorge" as we called it. We called it "black" because tens of people had perished in that defile. So this was one company -- these are not two locations, but one, and there is written "Donja Somanja." That in fact is the location Duganovic where there was deployed a combat group, the 243rd Mechanised Brigade, for securing the state border. And without any indication of Djeneral Jankovic, there is a circle, and that is actually a border post.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Just a second, General. At page 57, line 11 -- line 11, Your Honours, when you were referring to the Dulja Pass, you said it is one location, not two, because the transcript says it is two locations.

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The map shows two units, whereas it is one unit which is redeployed, and one can say, yes, two locations, but performing one mission under the agreement. It is all one facility which is securing the Crnojevska Gorge, it is one company, and that is how it is envisaged under the agreement.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: But to avoid any confusion, when you say "two locations," it is one location, but two places within this one location? Do I understand you correctly?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, linguistically, this is perhaps more correct, but we are talking about the same thing. This is about units which under the agreement are there. I'm telling you that this representation here is imprecise because this is just one unit. So I'm saying that all these units shown on this map are in conformity with the agreement for securing the state border, three locations as being assigned to units of company strength, and this here shows a border post which should not have been shown here. The Batlava Airport is also shown here, and that is not a location, a site, according to the agreement, but it is something according to the order for training and for securing the main road. And we also have the exercising ground near Vucitrn, so these are not at all the deployed parts of units beyond or in contravention of the agreement or violating that agreement, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Thank you, General. General, just take another look, because some of my colleagues feel that perhaps you omitted a location. I see a flag and the words -- the word "Zjum," Z-J-U-M. I don't know whether you mentioned that one.

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not mention that one. This is the, I should say, well-known combat group between Zjum and Zub of Major Vukovic, which was inspected daily by the verifiers and commended their conduct very much, also in terms of their treatment of the civilian population, and their assignment was the in-depth security of the state border.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Thank you, General. Tell us at this point, in view of the fact that you have given us all this information, how did the Pristina Corps Command react to this jeopardy to the state border and units in the border belt? We can start with the Kacanik area.

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Corps Command at that time, at the time when terrorism was spilling over to that area, was not alone, because already in the beginning of February, the forward -- a forward command post of the army was set up in Pristina, so the Command from Nis moved a part of its forces to Pristina. To specifically reply to your question, I would say that the Command of the Corps assessed the situation to be dramatic, extremely dangerous, and reacted in accordance with its powers, with their assessment -- and informed of its assessment in evaluation, the Command of the 3rd Army saying that the state border was in extreme peril, and it proposed specific measures. The Corps Command has no authority to do anything else on its own.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: To be more specific, let's look at 5D253 on e-court. General, this document, as we see, it says here: "Commander Lazarevic." Do you recognise it, "Pristina Corps Command, the 28th of February, 1999"?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I recognise both the document and what it says and the entire situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Can you explain to us, in brief, what this is about and what your proposal was?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I personally drafted this document, and I addressed it to the command post of the 3rd Army which was partly in Kursumlija, and the army commander, well, he was currently in Kursumlija, but his forward command post was in Pristina, which is why I addressed it to Kursumlija so that it would reach the army commander personally. And I am informing him in this document of the fact that there was a concentration of Siptar terrorists in the border belt on the Kacanik-Djeneral Jankovic-Doganovic-Globocica axis. These were strong terrorist forces, and in my assessment the task of these forces was to set up a corridor for the infiltration of terrorists from Macedonia and of weapons and military equipment. When I mentioned NATO, I was referring to NATO forces and their weapons. I further informed him of the fact that twice in February already there had been clashes with those terrorist forces. I informed him that there had been an attack by those terrorist forces on police forces and that there had been losses. One policeman was killed and five were wounded. Furthermore, what His Honour, the Presiding Judge asked me, I said that we had established that those special and specific forces, in view of their manner of action, their uniforms and NATO-supplied uniforms and equipment, that we felt that they had the support of NATO forces in Macedonia, and therefore, for the more efficient protection of the integrity of the state in that area for which the Pristina Corps was responsible, I proposed that in-depth security of the state border be strengthened and reinforced by sending a combat group from the 3rd Army, Combat Group 21, and resubordinating it to the Pristina Corps for the purposes of that task.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: And was that combat group resubordinated, and if so, when?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I recall, if I haven't forgotten, but I hope I haven't, that I sent this information to the chief of the General Staff of the Army of Yugoslavia personally, also to General Ojdanic for his information, and that very quickly an order followed from the General Staff to the Command of the 3rd Army, and then from the Command of the 3rd Army onwards, that this combat group should arrive as soon as possible in order to reinforce the security of the state border.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Thank you. General, tell us the following: We discussed this axis and these events. What was the operational situation that the Pristina Corps found itself in early 1999?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I beg Their Honours to bear with me and allow me to answer this question in a few sentences, because it's very hard to reply in just one sentence. The armed rebellion in Kosovo and Metohija was practically underway on the entire territory. Urban terrorism, violence greater than throughout 1998, 10 to 12 attacks a day, on the average, on the institutions of the system, the security forces and civilians. Six to seven persons lost their lives, on the average, due to terrorist attacks. So that's all about that. In the immediate vicinity of the Pristina Corps, around the territory of Kosovo and Metohija in Albania and Macedonia, there was a concentration of strong multinational forces from NATO, a concentration of exceptionally strong terrorist forces from all of Europe in Macedonia and Albania, and there were even entire brigades from America. These were US citizens of Albanian origin and American citizens. There was the Pristina Corps, which was mostly in its barracks. There were verifiers at every step with the corps units. The numbers of the Corps were less than in 1998 because there had been disengagement of their reinforcements. From the military aspect, my assessment was, and I'm telling you now, that the Pristina Corps, in March, found itself in a strategic trap, in military terms, because war and external aggression were imminent. It was only a matter of days when the Corps, which had only 10.000 men and which was in its barracks, would be destroyed within a few days, as had been announced, by mid-March.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, General. Your Honours, this might be a convenient moment for a break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, we'll break now and resume at 10 minutes to 1.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Bakrac.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: General, before the break we spoke about the operative position of the Pristina Corps. Could you now please tell me -- and we have seen before that one of the main tasks of the army was combat training of soldiers and units. So please tell me, in this period from the beginning of 1999 to the beginning of the war on the 23rd of May, 1999, how was combat training carried out?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Corps Command, in this operative situation, could do nothing else but to intensify the combat training of its units. With all the security limitations, organisational and technical and other limitations that existed at the lowest tactical level. What I'm trying to say is that in the period we are referring to, January to March 1999, over 25 per cent of the peacetime composition of the Corps was not trained for the tasks it was intended to perform, according to the training plan for the units, because from so-called "indirect mobilisation" or, rather, not "mobilisation" but "raising manpower levels," replenishment, they would get a certain number of men every month -- every three months, and these were trained only for basic tasks, how to behave in groups of soldiers up to squad level, which means a group of ten men. Everything higher up than that, how platoons, companies, battalions are engaged was something they knew nothing about. They didn't know how to handle collective weapons. They hadn't even seen those in the training centres they were trained in. So the brigades had to receive these men and conduct intensive training with combat equipment, artillery, armoured and mechanised equipment, anti-aircraft, infantry, and other equipment. They had to train them at close range and at the lowest tactical level. In a nutshell, the combat training plan envisaged the continuation of the training for a further three months, up to five months and 20 days. This was not just an order from the chief of the General Staff, although I remember such orders came, but it was the duty of every unit in the Army of Yugoslavia to continue intensive training for up to five months and 20 days. And to conclude, it was absolutely necessary, at the corps level in the garrisons, to conduct 50 to 60 exercises a month at the platoon-to-battalion levels.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, the plan of combat training is 5D1260, for your reference.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: This replenishment was -- with manpower was not against the agreement, was it?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. These were soldiers who were part of the establishment of the Corps, but as recruits they did not go straight to the corps units. Instead, they went to training centres. But these were our men, men intended for the Corps. After the completion of the first part of their training, they arrived in the brigades, where the second period of combat training was to commence.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: We heard here from Prosecution witness, Mr. Ciaglinski, also Mr. Crosland, that units of the Army of Yugoslavia carried out exercises at the time, manoeuvre exercises. Can you explain the difference between "manoeuvre" and "exercise"? These are two distinct terms.

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: By Their Honours leave, I'll try and explain it as briefly as possible. Exercising is a process repeating the same activities more than once. The content is always the same. A training exercise is an activity carried out according to a certain plan, certain dynamics, without repetition. One starts at 8.00 a.m., and the exercise is completed in the course of the day. If there are any errors, they are analysed, but they cannot be repeated within the scope of that task. Within the scope of exercises, there are exercises with a target practice and with live ammunition, and that is the duty of every unit and every brigade. With each new group of soldiers, a large number of live ammunition exercises have to be carried out, and there must be no mistakes because it's live ammunition. Throughout 1998, up to the war, the Pristina Corps did not carry out a single such exercise, and it should have carried out dozens of them. And now I arrive at the question as to what is a manoeuvre. Manoeuvres are large-scale exercises involving a number of branches of service at the level of the whole army. In the course of my military career, I never participated in a single manoeuvre carried out by the Yugoslav People's Army or the Army of Yugoslavia. As far as I can remember, in 1972, in Tito's time, there was a manoeuvre. It was called "Freedom 72." Truly, the term that was used here in evidence does not correspond to the truth. It is simply inconceivable, so that by saying that, I will conclude my answer. And I will also say that in relation to the plan and to what we were supposed to do at the level of our corps, we did less than 20 per cent of the basic training and basic exercises at the platoon and company level.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: I wanted to stop you there and to ask you a follow-up question, the number of exercises that were carried out. At what level were they carried out in 1998 and 1999 in the Pristina Corps?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: These were exercised carried out at platoon level, 40 to 60 men, and at the company level, 150 to 200 men. We didn't have any exercises at the battalion level, so we're talking about the lowest tactical level.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: In the course of these exercises, was the Army of Yugoslavia targeted by any attacks? And if "yes," by whom?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The exercises were carried out for the most part within the garrison training areas, but some of the exercises that were more peculiar, such as movements, had to be carried out along certain routes, roads. In most cases, those units were then targeted by the terrorist forces that were deployed in those areas, in the vicinity, or who had come into this area in order to provoke, to attack, and to prevent further training of the army.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: I just want to clarify one thing. General, kindly excuse me for this. Exercises, not military exercises, do not take place when the situation is tumultuous. Normally, these take place in times which are a little peaceful. So what was happening, and how do you describe this? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, you're entirely right. Exercises are part of peacetime training of soldiers, units and commands for the performance of their basic tasks. There are no exercises. It is difficult to carry out an exercise in a time of war. One exercises until the war starts. We're now talking about the exercises that were carried out in the period that preceded the aggression against the country and throughout 1998.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: General, if I understand you correctly, the exercises -- now we're talking about this period, and let me now complete my question. Up until the time when the war was declared, that's when the exercises were carried out at a certain place in the training area, enclosed area, but there was also a necessity for the army to exercise movement. Did OSCE monitors or verifiers monitor any of these exercises?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Every time a unit, a company-strength unit, would move out of the barracks, or every time a motorised unit comprising six or more vehicles would move, had to be reported to the OSCE mission. The OSCE mission then decided whether it would monitor those movements or whether this would be just for its information. And let me just add, when we're talking about those exercises, we had files with information about what we would be doing, how many people would be involved, and we would hand over those files to the OSCE mission in any given area. In most cases, the verifiers escorted those columns in their own vehicles, and very, very often they were present during the exercises, from the beginning to the end. I have reports from the units dating from that time period, indicating that very often, in particular in the Kosovska Mitrovica and Vucitrn areas, the verifiers expressed their satisfaction with what they had seen, what they had experienced, and with their presence at the exercises in general.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: At that time, did the General Staff of the Army of Yugoslavia take any measures to preserve the combat readiness in Pristina Corps?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it did take measures, and I know that one of the main concerns of the General Staff at that time was to monitor constantly the situation in Kosovo and Metohija, in other words, the combat readiness of the 3rd Army and of the Pristina Corps in particular. In addition to monitoring the situation, if I may just mention those measures in a couple of sentences, let me just say the following: I remember that at the beginning of March -- this is my personal experience, and we also heard evidence from participants in this activity -- that the chief of the General Staff himself headed a large team and they toured most of the Pristina Corps units. He was accompanied by the 3rd Army commander. I welcomed them, I briefed them, I submitted reports to them, and I was the person responsible for the combat readiness to the 3rd Army commander, and my next superior at the next level, the chief of the General Staff. So the chief of the General Staff and a large team verified the state of combat readiness. Some other activities on the part of the General Staff followed in order to improve the manning level in the Pristina Corps, and also the replenishment levels. I'm now talking about equipment.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: While we're dealing with this topic, could we please have Exhibit 3D750 up on the screen, please. Do you recognise this document, or, rather, could you please comment on this document? Is this one of the measures that were taken in order to improve the combat readiness or, rather, to maintain it as a certain level?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is an order issued by the chief of the General Staff of the Army of Yugoslavia, dated the 15th of March, to keep the soldiers who had started serving their national service in March, 1999 -- 1998, after they completed their national service in the ranks of the Pristina Corps for a further 30 days, it followed after a decision of the president of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia who was authorised under the law to make such a decision. So the March generation of soldiers, about 2.500 to 2.800 soldiers, were retained in the ranks of the Pristina Corps, and they were there when the war started.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: General, since most of the people on the left-hand side of the courtroom know that, but the others may not know, what do you mean when you say "the March generation"? Could you please explain to the Judges, how long did the national service last?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The national service lasted for 12 months, and this generation of soldiers had come in March 1998 to do their national service. They were supposed to be released --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I've done the same thing. There must be a different layout in this courtroom. I'm sorry for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, with all due respect, Your Honour, but I'm beginning to think it's intentional.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: General, I do apologise. Will you please repeat?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The March 1998 generation were supposed to be discharged in March 1999, between the 15th and the 20th of March. They were kept on the orders of the -- according to the decision of the president of the FRY.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Yes, we heard that. I just wanted you to clarify. The reason is because of the increased external pressure and the amassing of the foreign troops.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreters note, could the counsel please speak into the microphone.

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The strategic situation was extremely unfavorable. I use the term "strategic trap" for the Pristina Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: General, on the basis of this document, can we conclude that by the 15th of March, a week before NATO air strikes began, the soldiers were discharged from the national service and they left the Pristina Corps; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct. Even some of the March generation had been discharged until this order was issued, those who had been entitled to leave earlier because they had not used up all their leave. They had left the ranks of the Corps.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Is there a translation problem here? What was the point in keeping them within the Pristina Corps if they were allowed to leave before the war started?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. This document shows that on the 15th of March, seven days before NATO air strikes began, the General Staff of the Army of Yugoslavia issued a decision that the March intake that was supposed to be discharged after one year of national service should be kept in the army for another month because of an increased external pressure on the country and the amassing of foreign troops on the borders. And the General said that until the 15th, because the March intake had -- some of them had been already discharged, the remaining ones from that generation or intake were kept in the ranks of the Corps.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: If you look at page 70, line 11, your question is recorded as being: "Can we conclude that by the 15th of March, a week before the air strikes, the soldiers were discharged from national service and left the Pristina Corps?" In fact, just the opposite of that, is it?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. The point is, Your Honour, that until the 15th of March, 1999, there was a regular, usual procedure to discharge the soldiers who had completed their national service. They were not kept in their units. And the other to the opposite came in only on the 15th, to keep them there because of the increased danger for 30 more days. This concerned only a part of the March 1998 intake, because some of them had joined the Army before the 15th of March, 1998, and they had already been discharged.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: General, I have just one more question in this regard. We heard evidence here, and the Prosecutor argues, that the Army of Yugoslavia or the Pristina Corps had been preparing for a spring offensive. This fact, that up until the 15th, up until the very eve of the NATO air strikes, that the soldiers had been discharged from their national service as usual, does that correspond to any preparations for any kind of offensive?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreters note, the counsel is kindly asked to speak into the microphone. We cannot hear him.

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I explained the operative position of the Corps before the break. The Corps did not have the powers, the authority or the strength to prepare for any kind of spring offensive. The 3rd Army didn't do anything of the sort. The Army didn't do that, the General Staff didn't do that. There were just some minimum measures in place, and I'm sure that we will come to this topic soon. My answer is, no, when the war broke out, we were in a peacetime setup. We lived our daily lives in peace, as if there would not be a war in a hundred years.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Bakrac, do you have a microphone towards your right-hand side, because the --

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. I have my colleague's. Let me try it that way. Perhaps that would be a bit better, because if I talk to General Lazarevic, then of course this microphone doesn't really pick up my voice. Could we now have Exhibit 3D683 up in e-court. This is a document of the General Staff of the Yugoslav Army. It is also dated the 16th of March.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Can you give us your comment on what -- on the substance of this document?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is an order of the chief of the General Staff or, rather, his deputy in this particular case, and it constitutes a response to my request, or better to put it my proposal from the beginning of March to the effect that we needed to reinforce the in-depth security of the state border towards Macedonia. This order regulates resubordination to the 3rd Army of the Reconnaissance and Sabotage Battalion of the 72nd Specialists Brigade for the discharge of tasks according to the decision of the commander of the 3rd Army. And I'm duty-bound to say that even though that is what is written in this first item, this was not a reconnaissance and sabotage battalion, according to establishment numerical strength, but this was an ad hoc temporary formation, a small combat group, between 100 and 120 men strong. This order is in accordance or within the framework of our earlier-discussed matter on resubordination, how it was the General Staff -- the Chief of General Staff who would be the one to regulate resubordination, which would then entail my own order, and so on, and this is the entire process.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: General, at that time, sometime in that period when this build-up of troops and this danger was perceived, was any decision taken by the federal government in connection with the state border, and if so, what was it about?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The federal state, the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, followed from its own aspect a very close danger to the security of the country, and if I can remember, it was on the 5th of March that the federal government adopted a decision on expanding the border belt towards Macedonia and Albania approximately by 10 kilometres in order to make it possible for that area, for that border zone, to enable the engagement of units for the more efficient in-depth security and defence of the state border.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: In the framework of these measures that were imposed by the time, I should like to ask you to comment on a Prosecution exhibit, P1129. General, the exhibit is in front of you. Do you know what this document is?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that having toured and inspected the corps units by the chief of the General Staff, the chief of the General Staff and his team having done this control, there was an order to the Pristina Corps from the Army Command on the realisation of tasks which were issued by the chief of the General Staff. And now I see his order for the taking of additional measures, to build up and retain the combat readiness of the Corps from the 16th of March on.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: When you say "additional measures," can you comment on items 2 and 3?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Item 2 accentuates the measures to be taken to assess the adequacy, the adequacy of the forces for securing the state border, that is to say, it requires of us to see whether the engaged number is sufficient. Then it calls for a very specific activity. It requires of us to assess the adequacy of these separated units, in terms of sufficient supplies of ammunition, because it would become evident in the war later that we had problems with fire and with the adequacy of ammunition supplies. They were also required to pay specific attention to erecting barriers in the belt zone, in the areas which are defined in this item.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I'm sorry, you were. Could I have a clarification from counsel as to the exhibit number? It's in the transcript as "1129", but I don't have 1129 on my list. I don't know if it was misheard or mistranslated.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is a mistake, Your Honours. My learned colleague, perhaps I misspoke, but I do have it in front of you. It is P1921, Prosecution exhibit. That was the one that was announced.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Shall I continue?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Yes, please, what is in item 3?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In item 3, the chief of the General Staff demands intensified combat habilitation of the commands and units of the Pristina Corps as well as of other forces in the zone of responsibility of the Corps, and that it is his responsibility for carrying out missions, and that training should be adapted to specific conditions on the ground.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now look at page 3, item 12, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Just a brief comment on item 12, please.

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In item 12, the chief of the General Staff demands that intelligence and counter-intelligence measures be applied at all levels in order to protect units against attacks from terrorist forces from the area of Macedonia and Albania, but also in the area of Kosovo and Metohija, and towards the end of this item, he requires the efficient detection and frustration of terrorist activities, subversive and terrorist activities, counter-intelligence, the reconnaissance and subversive terrorist activities, towards the units of the Pristina Corps and the 3rd Army.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Item 16 on the next page, please can we have a very brief comment on that? What is being ordered there?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In item 16, the chief of the General Staff again returns to the task of intensified combat training -- of intensifying combat training, requiring that we intensify the training of specially set-up units and resubordinated units, as well as a part of the various specialties of reservists which were being trained at that time according to the annual planning, the Corps and Army units, and naturally orders that in that context, also through combat training, the morale of the members of our units be boosted in the process.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Were measures also taken at the level of the 3rd Army in order to step up combat readiness in March, to step up the combat readiness of the Pristina Corps in that month?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The 3rd Army Command monitored all these operative tasks from the General Staff, operationalised on further in practice by its own orders and commands and undertook additional measures within its ambit. Needless to say, everything that is written here had to be translated by the Command of the Army into its own orders, and later this was also done by the Corps, as was the case with other measures.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: General, can you look at 5D259. Exhibit 5D259. This is an order of the 3rd Army. I should like you to comment on item 1.

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The commander of the 3rd Army, from the forward command post in Pristina, where he was, ordered that due to the build-up of multinational forces within NATO in Macedonia and the compromising of security coming from that direction, that preparations be initiated for the execution of mobilisation of certain commands and units to be engaged in closing off axes and defending axes leading to the Republic of Macedonia or from the Republic of Macedonia and the Republic of Albania to the area of Kosovo and Metohija, and also orders that a part of these commands which are being engaged according to special plans, to reconnoiter these routes, these axes. So this is a preparatory order focusing on preparations for mobilising the forces that secure -- that protect the state border.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: General, would you now please take a look at 4D329 from the 20th of March, 1999. We are still talking about the peril to state territory, and in order to expedite matters can we now turn to page 2, item 6, and can I elicit your comment on that item?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is again an order from the 3rd Army commander. In the previous paragraphs, if I'm allowed to say so, warns again about the worsening of the security situation in Kosovo and Metohija and the general region. In paragraph 6, the army commander orders that preparations be made for a planned taking of defence positions once the signal or order has been received to do so, and there should be readiness to break up or route the terrorist forces and to defend against an aggression from Albania and Macedonia. So the army commander had all the relevant information at his disposal, and this is a preparatory order three or four days before the aggression, warning all the corps units to be ready to leave their peacetime locations as soon as possible and to stand ready to defend the country.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: We saw all those measures that were taken by the superior commands. How did the Pristina Corps Command implement all those measures to improve combat readiness? We saw the orders, we saw when they had come in. That was on the eve of the air strikes. What measures did you take?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Corps Command had the task to implement everything that had been ordered by the General Staff and by the 3rd Army Command through its orders, its plans, its instructions, and its actions; preparations for the mobilisation, preparations to man the sectors outside of the peacetime locations, preparations to defend the axes leading from Albania and Macedonia, to keep the soldiers from the March generation within its ranks and to include them in any tasks, and all other measures and activities.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Could you please look at P633. That's a Prosecution exhibit. It is a telegram. It is your telegram, in fact. The date is not quite clear, the 5th of March, 1999. It appears that in this document and in this telegram, you refer to the visit of the chief of the General Staff and part of the members of the General Staff. Could you please be so kind as to comment on this document?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This order was issued by me to the corps units just one day after the inspection and control by the chief of the General Staff and his team. I didn't wait for the instructions or orders from the Army Command, although these did follow and we did take some additional measures afterwards. But on the basis of what I personally observed in the course of that control visit, and on the basis of what the General Staff team observed, I ordered to the units to take additional measures. And in paragraph 1, I conveyed the assessment of the chief of the General Staff and his team, indicating that they were happy with the level of combat readiness observed in the Pristina Corps, in particular as to the level of training, morale and the command function, but bearing in mind, in light of the fact that the situation was deteriorating on a daily basis, I ordered that some additional measures be taken to disseminate the information about the deterioration of the situation to the entire Corps, to take measures to safeguard the personnel against any dangers, primarily terrorist attacks, and I can see it continues on to page 2.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I was just about to ask if we could move on to page 2 to complete the paragraph.

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I insisted that in the execution of these tasks, all the corps units should comply strictly with all the orders of the Corps Command and the Army Command in order to improve the overall level of the combat readiness, but at the same time I demanded that this order and all the information be disseminated to every single soldier, in terms of the forthcoming tasks.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: General, we have just enough time to deal with another document, 5D279. It's yet another order that you issued. It is dated the 23rd of March, 1999, on the eve of the air strikes. And then we will be completed. Do you recognise this order?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do. And as you can see, I drafted it myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: To make things clear for the Trial Chamber, you say, "as you can see." Where can we see it?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You can see it at the lower left-hand corner, my initials, "VL" that's the drafter, and "BV," that's the initials of the typist, and of course you can see my signature. I issued a brief order. This is a preparatory order to collate the recruitment plans, the mobilisation plans, that the units should themselves submit their proposals to the Corps Command. If an order for the mobilisation is issued for the mobilisation to be carried out successively, I was sure that the aggression would not take place so soon, but I was wrong, and my order was that they should submit to me by the 25th of March, 1999, their mobilisation plans. So what I mean to say is that the -- that we -- when the war broke out, we were in a peacetime formation.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: So this is the last sentence: "Submit proposals by the 25th of March, 1999"?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: And could you please now turn to paragraph 4. And paragraph 4, you forbid something here. Could you please explain that?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I prohibited the call-up of the reserve force or any kind of partial mobilisation of any personnel without my approval, because I did not have that power. I didn't have the power to do so. So I prohibited that. Let me just finish. This was not the preparation for a spring offensive.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, General. We have to end our work for today. Your Honours, I believe that this is a convenient moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Bakrac. Well, tomorrow we will be back in Court I, and that will be at 2.15, so we shall adjourn until then.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Thursday, the 8th day of November, 2007, at 2.15 p.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 1.47 p.m.,
